{{Short description|Type of positive integer}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
An '''amenable number''' is a positive [[integer]] for which there exists a [[multiset]] of as many integers as the original number that both add up to the original number and when multiplied together give the original number. To put it algebraically, for a positive integer ''n'', there is a multiset of ''n'' integers {''a''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''a<sub>n</sub>''}, for which the equalities
<math display="block"> n = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i = \prod_{i=1}^n a_i</math>
hold.<ref name=tamvakis/>

The amenable numbers were named in a 1995 problem posed by H. Tamvakis.<ref name=tamvakis>{{citation|last=Tamvakis|first=H.|title=Problem 10454|journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]|volume=102|page=463|year=1995|doi=10.2307/2975042 }}</ref> Whether a number is amenable can be determined from its value [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] 4.<ref name=solution/>

==Examples==
For example, 5 is amenable since 5 = 1 + (−1) + 1 + (−1) + 5.<ref>{{MathWorld|id=AmenableNumber|title=Amenable Number}}</ref>

The first few amenable numbers are<ref name=oeis/>
: 1, 5, 8, 9, 12, 13 ... {{OEIS|A100832}}.

==Characterization==
the amenable numbers consist exactly of the positive integers that are congruent to 0 or 1 [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] 4, and are not equal to 4.<ref name=solution>{{citation|first1=H.|last1=Tamvakis|first2=O.P.|last2=Lossers|title=Solution to Problem 10454. Amenable Numbers|journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]|volume=105|year=1998|page=368|doi=10.2307/2589724}}</ref>

For the integers of the form <math>n=4k+1</math>, where <math>k</math> is itself an integer, a solution can be given by a set of <math>2k</math> copies of <math>+1</math>, <math>2k</math> copies of <math>-1</math>, and one copy of <math>n</math>, generalizing the example of 5 given above. For the integers of the form <math>n=4k</math>, with <math>k>1</math>, a solution can be given by <math>n-2</math> copies of <math>\pm1</math> and one copy each of <math>\pm 2</math> and <math>2k</math>.<ref name=solution/>

Four can be shown not to be amenable by case analysis. For numbers <math>n</math> congruent to 2 mod 4, it is only possible for the product of <math>n</math> integers to equal <math>n</math> when there is a single even term, from which it follows that the sum of the terms is odd and therefore unequal to <math>n</math>. When <math>n</math> is congruent to 3 mod 4, all terms must be odd and there must be an odd number of terms congruent to 3 mod 4, from which it follows that the sum is 1 mod 4 and unequal to <math>n</math>.<ref name=solution/>

==Other properties==
It follows from their characterization that the set of amenable numbers is closed under multiplication: the product of two amenable numbers is an amenable number.<ref name=oeis>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A100832|name=Amenable numbers}}</ref>

==Related concepts==
Amenable numbers should not be confused with [[amicable number]]s, which are pairs of integers whose divisors add up to each other.
